text.title: Single Channel Bet Selector Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every Single Channel Bet Selector application MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The selection MUST be a written, dated, single-page rubric listing every candidate channel scored on the three named axes, stored where the founder will re-read it (version control or a dated doc). A verbal or chat-only decision ("SEO feels right") is not a selection and MUST NOT start the 90-day clock.

rationale.source: Gabriel Weinberg and Justin Mares, Traction (2015), Bullseye framework; widely established practice in decision journaling

rule.rationale: Solo founders fail by trying four channels poorly, and the failure is invisible because every pivot is justified verbally after the fact. A written rubric is what the founder grades against at week 12; without it the grading conversation is held against a memory that has already been edited to fit the outcome.

rule.statement: The rubric MUST score between 3 and 6 candidate channels, each drawn from a named channel taxonomy (Traction's 19 channels or an equivalent named list), with the channel written at the tactic level the founder would actually execute ("LinkedIn founder posts", "cold email to ops managers"), not at the category level ("social", "outbound").

rationale.source: Gabriel Weinberg and Justin Mares, Traction (2015), the 19 traction channels and the outer ring of Bullseye

rule.rationale: Fewer than 3 candidates means the rubric is ratifying a decision already made; more than 6 means the founder is deferring the decision into a spreadsheet. Category-level entries cannot be scored on founder fit because "social" is a dozen different weekly behaviours with different fit scores.

rule.statement: Each candidate MUST be scored 1 to 5 on exactly three axes with these definitions: founder_fit (will the founder execute the channel's weekly unit of work for 13 weeks without quitting), icp_density (share of paying customers or qualified conversations who already use or search in that channel), early_traction (has at least one unsolicited inbound lead or sale come from this channel). Axes MUST NOT be weighted, renamed or added to.

rationale.source: Gabriel Weinberg and Justin Mares, Traction (2015); this methodology's rubric definition

rule.rationale: Channel lists say what exists; they do not say which one this founder will still be doing in week 9. The three axes intersect what the founder will execute, where the ICP already is, and what has already worked once. Weighting reintroduces the founder's preference through the back door, which the rubric exists to remove.

rule.statement: The icp_density score MUST cite the sample it was read from: at least 5 paying customers or 50 qualified conversations, with the count of that sample observed in the channel written next to the score (for example "7 of 11 customers found us via LinkedIn"). A density score with no sample count MUST be recorded as 1.

rationale.source: This methodology's Applies If (5 paying customers or 50 qualified conversations); Rob Fitzpatrick, The Mom Test (2013) on evidence from real conversations

rule.rationale: Without the count, icp_density becomes "where I assume my customers are", which is usually where the founder already spends time. Forcing the fraction turns the axis into an observation about customers rather than a belief about the founder, and a 1 for "no data" is the honest score: a channel nobody has been observed in has no density evidence.

rule.statement: The chosen channel MUST score at least 12 of 15 in total AND at least 3 of 5 on every axis. A channel with a high total and one axis at 1 or 2 is rejected regardless of total. If no candidate clears both bars, the rubric MUST return "no bet" and route the founder to discovery or to instrumentation of the highest-scoring channel, not to a bet.

rationale.source: This methodology's rubric definition; widely established practice in multi-criteria gating (per-criterion minimums over weighted sums)

rule.rationale: A 5 / 5 / 2 channel spends 90 days discovering what the rubric already said: nobody has ever come through it. The per-axis floor stops the spreadsheet from rationalising a known-bad bet with two strong scores, and the explicit "no bet" outcome stops the founder from picking the least-bad option because the exercise felt like it owed them a winner.

rule.statement: The rubric MUST commit to exactly ONE channel for 90 days, name the start and end dates, and list the runner-up channels in a parking lot with their scores. During the 90 days the founder MUST NOT start or continue active work on a parked channel; passive presence (an existing profile, an unchanged website) is allowed, new weekly effort is not.

rationale.source: Gabriel Weinberg and Justin Mares, Traction (2015), Bullseye inner ring: focus on one channel

rule.rationale: Parallel pursuit destroys the per-channel signal: with three channels at a third of the effort each, none reaches the reps at which it compounds, and the week-12 grade cannot attribute the result. The written parking lot makes the trade-off visible and reversible at the grade instead of relitigated every Monday.

rule.statement: The 90-day plan MUST state the weekly unit of work in countable terms (3 LinkedIn posts per week, 100 cold emails per week, 2 podcast pitches per week) and two leading-indicator checkpoints at week 4 and week 8 with a numeric expectation each (replies, profile visits, demo requests). A checkpoint miss MUST trigger a written adjustment to execution, never a channel switch before week 12.

rationale.source: Gabriel Weinberg and Justin Mares, Traction (2015), on cheap tests before focus; widely established practice in leading vs lagging indicators

rule.rationale: Ninety days with only a week-12 number is a bet with no telemetry: by the time the founder learns the cold-email domain was burned in week 2, the quarter is gone. Countable weekly units also make founder_fit testable in retrospect, since "did I ship 3 posts a week" has a yes or no answer that "was I consistent" does not.

rule.statement: The plan MUST state, on the day of selection, a numeric kill criterion for week 12 (for example "fewer than 10 qualified demo requests AND fewer than 1 paying customer by the end date means the bet failed") and the action that follows (re-run the rubric with the result as new early_traction evidence). The criterion MUST NOT be revised during the 90 days; a revision is recorded as a failed bet.

rationale.source: Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer, The Psychology of Sunk Cost (1985); Gabriel Weinberg and Justin Mares, Traction (2015)

rule.rationale: Without a pre-committed exit the bet either drags on indefinitely or is abandoned quietly, and in both cases the rubric never gets its most valuable input: a channel with real traction data. Sunk-cost pressure peaks exactly at week 12, so the only number the founder can trust then is the one written down at week 0.

section.title: Conclusion targets used by the decision tree

rule.statement: Run the full procedure; emit an artefact passing the output contract.
rule.rationale: Terminal target used by 06-decision-tree when a channel clears the rubric.

rule.statement: Skip; surface the missing precondition; do not synthesize.
rule.rationale: Terminal target used by 06-decision-tree when a channel already produces revenue or no ICP signal exists.
